title: THE KING WHO STARTED WITH GOD… THEN STOPPED TRUSTING HIM
paragraphs:
THE KING WHO STARTED WITH GOD… THEN STOPPED TRUSTING HIM
The Warning Hidden in Asa’s Final Years: You Can Have Decades of Faithfulness Behind You—and Still Let Your Heart Drift in the Final Miles
There is something more frightening than watching a wicked man reject God.
It is watching a man who once trusted God slowly learn how to live without depending on Him.
That is what makes the final years of King Asa so uncomfortable.
Because Asa was not always rebellious.
He was not introduced to us as an idol-loving pagan who wanted nothing to do with God.
He knew what it was like to pray when the odds were impossible.
He knew what it was like to watch God answer.
He knew what revival looked like.
He tore down idols.
He confronted spiritual corruption.
He called a nation back toward the LORD.
He even removed his own grandmother Maacah from her royal position because she had made a detestable image for Asherah.
This was not casual religion.
Asa had history with God.
And that is precisely why his ending should make every longtime Christian uncomfortable.
Because somewhere between the miracles of his earlier years and the grave waiting at the end of his forty-one-year reign, something changed.
Not necessarily his vocabulary.
Not his religious résumé.
Not the memories people had of him.
His dependence changed.
And perhaps the most dangerous spiritual drift is the kind that happens after you already have enough victories behind you to believe you could never drift.
Read slowly.
Because Asa’s story may not merely be about a dead king.
It may be about us.
Years earlier, an enormous army came against Judah.
The situation looked humanly impossible.
And Asa knew exactly what to do.
He cried to the LORD.
His prayer in 2 Chronicles 14 is stunning because there is almost no swagger in it. Asa does not pretend Judah is stronger than it is. He does not present God with his military credentials.
He essentially confesses:
We need You.
There is no one like You to help the powerless against the mighty.
So help us.
That was Asa when he was desperate.
That was Asa when he knew he could not save himself.
And God delivered him.
Then came reform.
Renewal.
Covenant.
The people sought the LORD.
Second Chronicles 15 says that they entered into covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart and soul.
Asa even removed idols from the land.
For years, his life seemed to declare:
God is enough.
Then another crisis came.
Baasha king of Israel moved against Judah and fortified Ramah.
Asa had a problem.
But this time Asa did not respond like the Asa of earlier years.
He had learned something dangerous.
He had learned how to solve problems.
He took silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the king’s house and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Aram, seeking a political and military alliance.
And here is what makes the story terrifying.
It worked.
At least immediately.
Ben-hadad attacked Israel.
Baasha abandoned his building project at Ramah.
Asa mobilized Judah and carried away the stones and timber.
Problem solved.
Except heaven did not call it success.
Hanani the seer came to Asa with a diagnosis far deeper than military strategy.
The Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 16:7 exposes the issue:
“בְּהִשָּׁעֶנְךָ עַל־מֶלֶךְ אֲרָם וְלֹא נִשְׁעַנְתָּ עַל־יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ”
Bəhishsha’enkha ‘al-melekh Aram, wəlo nish‘anta ‘al-YHWH Elohekha…
The heart of the accusation is devastating:
Because you relied upon the king of Aram and did not rely upon the LORD your God.
That Hebrew idea of leaning or relying is exactly where Asa’s battle was being fought.
Not merely on a battlefield.
In his heart.
What was he leaning on?
That question reaches across the centuries and walks directly into our lives.
What are you leaning on now?
Not what did you lean on when you first believed.
Not what did you lean on during the crisis ten years ago.
Not what does your testimony say you once trusted.
What are you leaning on now?
Your income?
Your savings?
Your intelligence?
Your connections?
Your reputation?
Your ministry?
Your spouse?
Your doctor?
Your pastor?
Your own ability to manipulate circumstances until everything works again?
None of those things is necessarily evil.
The danger begins when a gift becomes the place where dependence that belongs to God is transferred.
Asa’s strategy succeeded politically while exposing him spiritually.
That is one of the most dangerous truths in this entire story:
Something can work and still reveal that your heart is wandering from God.
The deal can close.
The money can arrive.
The relationship can happen.
The strategy can succeed.
The audience can grow.
The problem can disappear.
And heaven can still be asking:
Why did you stop leaning on Me?
Then Hanani says words that should be burned into the heart of every believer:
“כִּי יְהוָה עֵינָיו מְשֹׁטְטוֹת בְּכָל־הָאָרֶץ לְהִתְחַזֵּק עִם־לְבָבָם שָׁלֵם אֵלָיו”
“For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose heart is whole toward Him.”
Second Chronicles 16:9.
The Hebrew phrase ləvavam shalem elav carries the sense of a heart that is whole, complete, undivided toward Him.
God was not wandering the earth desperately searching for impressive people.
He was looking for hearts fully turned toward Him.
And Asa had once been that man.
That is what hurts.
He knew.
He had seen.
He had experienced.
He had testimony.
And when God sent someone to confront the drift, Asa had another opportunity.
Repent.
Break.
Remember.
Come home.
Instead, he became angry.
Second Chronicles 16:10 says Asa was enraged with Hanani and put him in prison.
Think about the tragedy.
The king who once removed idols now removed the voice confronting his own idol.
That is how spiritual decline often progresses.
First, we stop depending upon God.
Then God exposes it.
Then instead of hating the sin, we begin hating whatever exposed it.
A sermon suddenly feels “too judgmental.”
A faithful friend becomes “negative.”
A biblical correction becomes “toxic.”
A Scripture passage becomes something we explain away.
Conviction begins feeling like an enemy because something inside us no longer wants to surrender.
And perhaps someone reading this has reached that place.
You still love Christian content—as long as it comforts you.
You still want Jesus—as long as He does not touch the thing you refuse to surrender.
You still want grace—as long as repentance is not required.
But Jesus did not come merely to decorate the life we refuse to surrender.
He came as Lord.
And grace does not merely soothe sinners.
Grace transforms them.
The story becomes even darker.
Asa did not only imprison Hanani. Scripture says he oppressed some of the people at that time.
That detail matters.
A heart resisting God rarely damages only itself.
Eventually someone nearby gets hurt.
Our pride leaks.
Our bitterness leaks.
Our secret sin leaks.
Our refusal to repent leaks.
The people closest to us eventually begin living with the consequences of battles we refuse to bring before God.
Then comes one of Scripture’s saddest descriptions of a man approaching the end.
“In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa was diseased in his feet, and his disease became severe…”
Then the Chronicler adds the sentence that changes everything.
The Hebrew says:
“וְגַם־בְּחָלְיוֹ לֹא־דָרַשׁ אֶת־יְהוָה כִּי בָּרֹפְאִים”
Wəgam-bəḥolyo lo-darash et-YHWH, ki barof’im.
Even in his sickness, he did not seek the LORD, but the physicians.
Do not misuse this passage.
The biblical point is not that receiving medical treatment is sinful.
Scripture does not require Christians to reject physicians, medicine, hospitals, surgery, or legitimate medical care. The problem is explicitly stated in the verse:
“לֹא־דָרַשׁ אֶת־יְהוָה”
Lo darash et-YHWH.
He did not seek the LORD.
The tragedy was not simply that doctors were present.
The tragedy was that dependence upon God was absent.
The physicians became another chapter in the pattern already exposed by Hanani.
Earlier it was Syria.
Now it was physicians.
Different crisis.
Same heart problem.
Asa kept reaching horizontally without first bowing vertically.
And suddenly the story becomes painfully modern.
Because we do this too.
Something breaks and we Google before we pray.
Someone hurts us and we message everybody except God.
Money gets tight and anxiety becomes our counselor.
Our body becomes sick and we can spend hours researching symptoms while barely spending minutes pouring our fear before the Father.
Our marriage begins cracking and we obsess over changing the other person while refusing to let Christ expose us.
We feel empty, so we scroll.
Lonely, so we seek attention.
Ashamed, so we hide.
Afraid, so we control.
Wounded, so we numb ourselves.
And eventually we can become extremely skilled at surviving without actually seeking God.
That may be the warning hidden in Asa’s final years.
You can remember what dependence felt like while no longer living dependent.
You can tell stories about answered prayers while barely praying now.
You can sing worship songs about surrender while secretly controlling everything.
You can defend biblical truth publicly while resisting biblical correction privately.
You can have thirty years of testimony behind you and still need repentance today.
Yesterday’s faithfulness cannot substitute for today’s surrender.
Asa eventually died in the forty-first year of his reign.
A king who had experienced extraordinary movements of God finished his recorded story beneath a haunting sentence:
He did not seek the LORD.
But this is where Asa’s story forces us to look beyond Asa.
Because if Scripture only exposed failing human kings, we would be left with despair.
We need another King.
A King who would never drift.
A King whose heart would remain perfectly obedient to His Father.
A King who would not merely call His people back to God but would actually bear their sins and bring them to God.
Jesus Christ.
Where Asa failed, Christ remained faithful.
Where human kings stumble, Jesus does not.
Where we have trusted ourselves, Christ calls us to repent.
Where we have hidden sin, Christ brings truth into darkness.
Where guilt says, “You have gone too far,” the cross announces that the blood of Jesus is sufficient for sinners who come to Him.
This is the Gospel.
Not “try harder so God will finally tolerate you.”
Not “pretend you never drifted.”
Not “hide your scandal until everyone forgets.”
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Christ was crucified for sinners.
He bore sin.
He died.
He rose again.
And everyone who truly comes to Him in repentant faith finds something scandalous in its beauty:
Grace.
Maybe your story has become messy.
Maybe you knew God deeply once.
Maybe there was a season when prayer was oxygen and Scripture felt alive, but now you barely recognize the person you have become.
Maybe nobody knows.
You still post the verse.
Still say “God bless.”
Still attend church.
Still know exactly when to say amen.
But inside?
Something has moved.
You stopped seeking.
And perhaps God allowed you to reach this article because He is not finished confronting what He intends to redeem.
Do not respond like Asa responded to Hanani.
Do not imprison the message because it hurts.
Let it hurt.
Let Scripture search you.
Let the Holy Spirit expose what you have been leaning on.
And then run toward Christ.
There is still mercy.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still a cross.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still grace for the person who finally stops pretending.
The warning of Asa is not “one failure and God throws you away.”
The warning is far more searching:
Do not become so hardened that when God exposes your misplaced trust, you refuse to return.
Repentance is not humiliation for humiliation’s sake.
It is the doorway back into fellowship.
Maybe the prayer you need tonight is not eloquent.
Maybe it is simply:
“Jesus, I have been leaning on everything except You. Forgive me. Bring my heart home.”
Someone else reading those words may discover they are not the only believer fighting their way back toward wholehearted dependence upon Christ.
And please do not keep this message trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “share” proves someone is a better Christian. It does not.
We glorify God through lives of faith, obedience, love, truth, worship, and good works flowing from His grace.
But if this biblical warning helped you, sharing it can become one simple way of putting truth in front of someone who may desperately need it.
Someone who once burned brightly.
Someone quietly drifting.
Someone still wearing the language of faith while learning to survive without dependence upon God.
Finish with Jesus.
There are truths you do not save because you have forgotten them. You save them because you know how easily the heart can forget.
The Gospel cannot be bought. Salvation is the gift of God through Christ.
But supporting Christian work can be a practical expression of generosity when you genuinely believe that work is helping spread biblical truth.
And there is more.
If these messages strengthen you, help us place them in front of someone else.
Save the messages you know you will need again.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because sometimes confession begins when somebody finally has the courage to stop pretending.
Asa’s story began with a man who knew how desperately he needed God.
His final years warn us what can happen when a person with yesterday’s testimony stops living with today’s dependence.
So do not merely ask:
“How did Asa end up there?”
Ask the harder question.
What am I leaning on now that has quietly taken the place where only God belongs?
Bring the answer to Jesus.
Because your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
The King who carried a cross still receives repentant sinners, restores wandering hearts, forgives the guilty, and turns stories of shame into testimonies of grace.
And perhaps that is the sentence worth carrying with you long after this page closes:
Do not spend your final years living on memories of a God you once trusted—when Jesus is calling your heart to trust Him again today.
